title: Women, Race & Class
author: Angela Y. Davis
target_audience: Students and scholars of feminist theory and history
Anyone interested in the intersections of race, class, and gender
Activists and organizers in social justice movements
General readers seeking to understand the complexity of feminism in America
core_themes: The intersectionality of gender, race, and class in the women’s movement
The historical relationship between feminism, abolition, and the civil rights movement
The exclusion and marginalization of Black women and women of color in the mainstream feminist movement
Labor movements and their connections to women’s rights
The relationship between reproductive justice and social oppression
primary_purpose: To critically examine the evolution of the women’s liberation movement in the United States, highlighting how race and class have shaped struggles for women’s rights and revealing the historical contributions and unique challenges faced by Black women and other marginalized groups.

structure_format.narrative_style: Analytical, scholarly, historical with a critical perspective
structure_format.organization: 12 chapters organized chronologically and thematically, each focusing on key periods or issues (e.g., slavery, suffrage, labor)
features: Rigorous historical research using primary sources
Critical examination of well-known feminist figures and mainstream movements
Contextual analysis of major social and political movements
Interweaving of personal histories, biographies, and collective activism

key_concepts_lessons: The feminist movement’s history is deeply intertwined with issues of race and class, and cannot be understood in isolation.
Black women and women of color have played pivotal but often overlooked roles in social reform movements.
Mainstream (white, middle-class) feminism has frequently marginalized or excluded women of color and working-class women.
Struggles for civil rights, labor rights, and reproductive justice are interconnected.
Genuine progress for women requires coalition-building and recognizing intersecting oppressions.
Critical reflection on historical narratives is necessary to avoid repeating patterns of exclusion.
style_tone: Accessible for academic and lay readers
notable_features: Foundational text on intersectional feminism (avant la lettre)
Balances detailed historical analysis with critical theory
Features case studies and profiles of key Black women activists
Highly influential in feminist, Black studies, and radical political circles
cultural_historical_context: Published at the dawn of intersectional theory, Davis’s book responded to the feminist movement’s increasing self-critique over race and class exclusion in the 1970s. It draws upon the legacies of abolition, civil rights, and socialist feminism within the context of US history, written by a prominent activist-intellectual with firsthand experience of the movements chronicled.
reception_impact: Widely acclaimed as a groundbreaking and essential feminist text
Frequently assigned in university courses on gender, race, and American history
Credited with paving the way for the concept of intersectionality in feminist theory
Praised for its rigorous scholarship and readability
Subject of ongoing debate regarding strategies for solidarity and inclusivity in feminist movements
comparable_titles: Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism by bell hooks
This Bridge Called My Back: Writings by Radical Women of Color edited by Cherríe Moraga and Gloria E. Anzaldúa
The Second Sex by Simone de Beauvoir (for broader feminist theory)
